document_check.note: Crocco EA, Curiel RE, Kitaigorodsky M, Grau GA, Garcia JM, Duara R, Barker W, Chirinos CL, Rodriguez R, Loewenstein DA. Intrusion errors and progression of cognitive deficits in older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and PreMCI states. Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2021;50(2):135-142, doi:10.1159/000512804 (PMC author manuscript, 17 pages including Tables 1 to 5). The cited numbers are in the document: AUC .905 for Cued B1 (Table 2, p14; text p6), AUC .919 for Cued B2 (p7), and the Youden cut-point of .44 with sensitivity 83.3% and specificity 86.3% (p6). The four analysed groups are Stable CN (n=51), PreMCI Non-Progressors (n=25), PreMCI Progressors (n=22) and aMCI Progressors to dementia (n=18) (Table 1, p13); there is no aMCI non-progressor group, as the review states.

cited_result: AUC 0.905 (Cued B1 PIE ratio; 0.919 for Cued B2) for separating Stable cognitively normal participants from aMCI participants who progressed to dementia. The Youden cut-point of .44 gave sensitivity 83.3% and specificity 86.3%. Principal result appraised: the Cued B1 AUC of .905 (Stable CN n=51 against aMCI Progressors n=18).
tool_reason: The cited AUC evaluates one baseline measure (the LASSI-L intrusion ratio) against the later outcome of progression to dementia or stable normal cognition over a mean 26.5 months, which under the operator's clarification 2 of 2026-09-29 is a prognostic factor question (QUIPS), not a diagnostic-accuracy design and not a multivariable model.

domains.rationale: Convenience recruitment from two research cohorts with no count of eligible or invited persons, no participation rate and no recruitment period. Decisively, the cited AUC is computed on a sample selected on the outcome: Stable CN participants had to be normal at both baseline and final follow-up, and the aMCI group contains only those who progressed to dementia. aMCI non-progressors and people who declined from normal cognition are not in the analysis, so the analysed sample does not represent any population in which the factor would be used to predict progression. Exclusion criteria are announced but never listed.

signalling.quote: We recruited 116 older adults who participated in either the 1Florida Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC), Clinical Core at Mount Sinai Medical Center, Miami Beach, Florida, or as part of an RO1 study on cognitive aging funded by the National Institute of Health (Dr. Loewenstein, Principal Investigator) at the University of Miami, Miller School of Medicine.

domains.rationale: No information on how many people were enrolled at baseline versus how many had a follow-up evaluation, on losses, reasons for loss, or differences between completers and non-completers. Follow-up ranged from 10 to 40 months. Figure 1 (initial and final disposition) is not reproduced in the text. Because inclusion in the analysed groups required a qualifying follow-up diagnosis, anyone lost to follow-up is invisible; whether this distorts the association cannot be judged from the report.

signalling.question: Are all baseline diagnostic groups accounted for at follow-up?
signalling.quote: The above classifications resulted in four groups: 1) Stable CN, 2) PreMCI Progressors who progressed to a formal diagnosis of aMCI, 3) PreMCI Non-Progressors, who remained PreMCI, or reverted to a diagnosis of CN, 4) aMCI Progressors, who progressed to dementia during follow-up.

domains.rationale: The PIE ratio is defined by an explicit formula, measured at baseline with the same instrument in both studies, in the participant's preferred language, and reported as a continuous variable (group means in Table 1); the AUC uses the continuous measure. Reliability data are not given in this paper and missing data on the factor are not reported, but nothing suggests differential measurement. The cut-points were optimised in the same data; this affects the accompanying sensitivity and specificity and is addressed under domain 6.

signalling.question: A clear definition or description of the prognostic factor is provided
signalling.quote: The ratio is denoted as follows: Total Intrusion Errors/ (Total Intrusion Errors + Total Correct Responses) for LASSI-L Cued B1 (a measure of susceptibility to PSI) and LASSI-L Cued B2 recall (a measure of recovery from PSI).

signalling.question: Method of prognostic factor measurement is adequately valid and reliable
signalling.quote: Participants are tested in their preferred language (English versus Spanish). The LASSI-L has been shown to be culturally fair in either language [29].

signalling.question: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points are used
signalling.answer: Yes for the AUC (continuous); No for the cut-points (data-derived)
signalling.quote: ROC analyses were employed using Youden’s criteria, which revealed sensitivity, specificity, and an area under the ROC curve to determine optimal cut-points for Cued B1 and Cued B2 that successfully distinguished Stable CN from aMCI participants that had progressed to dementia.

signalling.question: The method and setting of measurement of the prognostic factor is the same for all study participants
signalling.quote: As part of the testing protocol, all participants were administered the Loewenstein-Acevedo Scales for Semantic Interference and Learning (LASSI-L), which was not used for diagnostic classification to avoid potential circularity.

signalling.question: Was the prognostic factor measured before the outcome occurred?
signalling.quote: The present results indicated that baseline intrusion error rates on Cued B1 and Cued B2 recall on the LASSI-L could differentiate stable cognitive normal from aMCI progressors to dementia over 26.5 months

signalling.question: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for the prognostic factor
signalling.quote: Searched Methods, Results and Table 1 for missing LASSI-L data or per-variable n; Table 1 reports PIE means by group without stating how many had the measure.

signalling.question: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing prognostic factor data
signalling.quote: No mention of missing data or imputation anywhere in the text.

domains.rationale: Dementia and stable normal cognition are defined by explicit CDR and neuropsychological criteria applied identically in both studies at annual evaluations, and the LASSI-L was deliberately excluded from diagnostic classification. Blinding of diagnosticians to LASSI-L scores is implied rather than stated, and the outcome was ascertained at variable follow-up times (10 to 40 months), but follow-up did not differ between groups.

signalling.question: A clear definition of the outcome is provided
signalling.quote: The criteria for dementia used in both studies was a Global CDR of 1.0 or greater, indicating functional deficits, and neuropsychological performance on memory tests that were 2.0 SD or greater, below normal limits for age, education, and language group.

signalling.question: Method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable
signalling.quote: The neuropsychological assessment batteries used for diagnostic purposes were identical, as is the clinician-administered standard clinical assessment protocol, including the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale (CDR) [18] and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) [20].

signalling.question: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants
signalling.quote: Both studies are longitudinal investigations using identical assessment methods and diagnostic criteria, including annual clinical and neuropsychological evaluations.

signalling.question: Was the outcome determined without knowledge of the prognostic factor?
signalling.quote: To avoid any circularity in the argument, the LASSI-L was not employed in diagnostic classification.

signalling.question: Was the timing of outcome assessment similar across groups?
signalling.quote: The average follow-up interval between study groups was 26.5 months, and there were no differences between groups when it comes to average follow-up.

domains.rationale: The two groups in the cited AUC differ by baseline diagnosis by design (aMCI with CDR 0.5 and impaired delayed recall against CN with CDR 0 and normal testing) and by age (76.2 against 70.6 years, p=.001). The ROC is unadjusted; the covariates of the stated analyses of covariance are not named; and the claim that age, sex and ethnicity did not influence the results comes from post-hoc analyses reported without data. The association of the intrusion ratio with later dementia therefore cannot be separated from baseline cognitive status and age, so the prognostic association is very likely distorted.

signalling.question: All important confounders are measured
signalling.quote: As depicted in Table 1, Stable CN participants were younger (70.6 years; SD = 6.9) than the PreMCI Progressors (77.1 years; SD 6.9) and the aMCI Progressors (76.2 years; SD = 6.9). As expected, the aMCI Progressors had lower average MMSE scores than the other three groups (who had equivalent MMSE scores).

signalling.question: Clear definitions and valid, reliable measurement of the confounders; same method for all
signalling.quote: Age (Range: 57–91) ... Education (Range: 6–22) ... % Female ... % Hispanic ... MMSE Total Score (Range: 21–30)

signalling.question: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design
signalling.quote: had a Global CDR scale score of 0.5; d) impaired delayed recall (i.e., 1.5 SD or greater, below normal limits for age, education, and language group for either the HVLT-R or delayed paragraph recall from the NACC UDS.

signalling.question: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis
signalling.quote: In additional post-hoc analyses, we found no evidence in this study that Hispanic ethnicity, age, or sex influenced the obtained results, consistent with our recent findings [29] and demonstrating that the LASSI-L is equally effective diagnostically among Hispanics and non-Hispanics.

signalling.question: Are the covariates of any adjusted analysis stated?
signalling.quote: We employed a series of one-way analyses of variance and covariance for interval level variables for the initial comparisons between groups with different patterns of cognitive decline or recovery (e.g., progression to MCI or dementia, reversion to normal cognition).

signalling.question: Appropriate imputation methods for missing confounder data
signalling.quote: No mention of missing confounder data or imputation.

domains.rationale: The Cued B1 AUC is reported with its standard error and 95% confidence interval, and ROC analysis is suitable for a single factor. However, the cut-points were chosen by Youden's index in the same small sample (51 against 18) with no internal validation, so the cited sensitivity and specificity are optimistic; the Cued B2 AUC is given without a confidence interval; there is no protocol; ROC analysis was reported only for the extreme contrast; post-hoc analyses are asserted without data; and the tables and text are inconsistent in places (see notes).

signalling.question: Sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis strategy
signalling.answer: Probably yes (Cued B1); Probably no (Cued B2)

signalling.question: Cued B2 AUC reported with a measure of precision
signalling.quote: (.919; p<.001). Using Youden’s criteria, a cut-point of.24 (PIE ratio for Cued B2) yielded a sensitivity of 88.9% and specificity of 86.3%.

signalling.question: Strategy for model building is appropriate and based on a conceptual framework
signalling.quote: Single factor evaluated in a univariable ROC analysis: 'We derived the optimal cut-point that distinguished our Stable CN group and aMCI Progressors using ROC analyses.'

signalling.question: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design (including optimism of data-derived cut-points)
signalling.quote: Using Youden’s criteria, a cut-point of.44 (PIE ratio on Cued B1) yielded a sensitivity of 83.3% and specificity of 86.3% [See Figure 1].

signalling.question: Is the sample size adequate for stable estimates?
signalling.quote: Limitations of the current findings were modest sample sizes and a lack of neuroimaging to determine how proactive interference intrusion errors tracked with amyloid deposition and volumetric loss.

signalling.question: No selective reporting of results
signalling.quote: Post-hoc tests revealed that among those diagnosed as PreMCI Clinical versus PreMCI Neuropsychological, the percentage of proactive interference semantic intrusion errors was equally effective in predicting progression to MCI or reversion to CN.

overall: High risk of bias (QUIPS): study participation high, study attrition moderate, prognostic factor measurement low, outcome measurement low, study confounding high, statistical analysis and reporting moderate.
overall_rationale: By the QUIPS rule any high domain makes the overall high; two domains are high. The cited AUC compares two outcome-selected extreme groups (normal at both time points against aMCI participants who all converted), so participation is high risk, and the groups differ by baseline diagnosis and age with no adjustment, so confounding is high risk. The factor and the outcome are otherwise well defined and measured, but attrition is unreported and the Youden cut-points are optimised in the same small sample without validation. The AUC therefore largely reflects the cross-sectional separation of aMCI from normal cognition and overstates the factor's ability to predict progression.
